Mercer clicked on the Cascade Precinct total. The unofficial count had voted it "no." He called the sheriff's station in Cascade, to say that he'd made a mistake with Claire Weiss.

In the household ledgers of marriage, it is not a husband's fault if money goes missing. Nor is it a husband's crime to have the wrong county on his driver's license. And in the double conspiracies that form in the stilled, sleepless moments after a murder, a man will never, ever accuse his wife. On the rainy morning of November 17, Mercer still believed in his wife's innocence. He had voted "no" against himself. He had believed. But now he thought about the clinical tone in which Claire had first learned of the measure's defeat: "That's too bad." All the nurses said she had the same level expression whenever one of her patients died. And, odder still, she had a certain exactness in the way she skipped parts of the story with the nurse in the park. She'd been so inexact in her story about Gregory Fraser.

Put enough odd stickers on a page, and they can start to connect. He called his wife at home and said he was coming to the house. She said she'd iron his shirts.

On February 5, 2013, the Monday before Valentine's Day a week-and-a-half after I started working as a newspaper reporter, my editor gave me the morning obituaries to write.

The first was eighty-two-year-old Sherman Blackwell of Center, Nevada.

I ran a Google search for "Sherman Blackwell Center Nevada" and came up with links to an area conference on "action sports and outdoor recreation" something called the Center/Northeastern Nevada Economic Summit. The conference had a long list of local sponsors who, I guessed, might be able to tell me some things.

At the top of the list of sponsors was something called the Blackwell Fund for Enterprise, in honor of the late Sherman Blackwell. It had paid for an airline-scale banner with Blackwell's image over the entrance of the conference center.

"I believe in value of place," read the photo caption. "Sometimes shareholders win, and sometimes they lose."

Then I checked out the rest of the list.

I drove two hours southwest, over the mountains, to the Blackwell property, the modest cluster of houses, one five and the others falling away from it, sitting at the open end of the narrow valley, like a comet in its tail. Today's generation of Blackwells lived in the big house at the heart ofthe landowning dynasty that stretched back to gold-rush days. There was an old wooden storage shed toward the back, and a corrugated-tin outbuilding on cinderblocks across the yard. The yard itself was gravel and dust, the road beyond it leading toward Rattlesnake, twenty miles from the paved world.

If Grant County as a whole has treated the Blackwells with far-flung reverence, and endowed Sherman Blackwell with grandfatherly local-hero status, then here on the Rawhide River, in the family fortress, Blackwell has been nothing less than exalted. One vote in a thousand. He punched some numbers into the calculator. That was somewhere around a six-million-to-one chance. He pulled out a coin from the jar on his desk. The last time I flipped it, it came up heads, he thought as he wrenched himself up out of his chair. Irritated, he went to the door and flipped the coin twenty-nine more times before he went upstairs to see his wife.

Morning broke over the Philpott home like any other Election Day. Mr. Philpott made himself a Cheerios-and-raisin tea breakfast, and after Heather got the kids on the bus, she took a random-order DNA test.

The Los Angeles Police Department had asked private labs to extract DNA from a hundred empty water bottles- Heineken, Herbal Essences, Dasani, and Hi-C, smuggled out of bins and abandoned at the periphery of crime scenes-to look to see if they could identify the people who had left them. Heather Philpott took that to mean that everybody had DNA on everything, so she decided to find out everything she could about her own.

Mr. Philpott had a bigger theory. He reckoned God wanted him to set Heather's mind straight, and the DNA test was just what he needed to do it. The room went dark two days earlier than planned. Mercer pulled the plug at midnight on January 2, when the snowstorm was forecast to settle, the roads closed, and ambulances couldn't make it to Bend. He pulled out not because of any foolish hope they could change their minds and vote it back in -- he knew better -- but simply because a doctor was an officer of the law, and it was his duty. He had already sent a list of patients to the hospital in Bend and booked the last flights out tomorrow. At 5 a.m. he would send someone to lock the doors.

On the radio a jazz track was playing, with a sweep over the trebles and a wistful sax in the back:
Another city, A different crowd, A different town
You can't slow down, You got to have a reason
You got to keep on moving

Mercer studied the small group around the table, to see if anyone had started to cry yet. They'd known since last night that this would happen, but some people always cried more over the end than others did over the beginning.

As he stirred the mugs of hot cider, the last burst of the song finished:
They say this is a goodbye, I know it's not
To the part that still burns
I gotta walk off ... ... the last burn
Gonna walk until the last ...
I gotta walk off ...

The young man at the other end of the table touched the shoulder of the man beside him. The young man was tall, blondish, and handsome in a screamy-rock-star kind of way, though in Mercer's world he may as well have stepped off the stage at tonight's Eagles concert. The man on his left was Larry Roulund, forty-two, son of a local farmer, back from Dallas to care for his mother after his father's death, out of dairy farming himself after most of the farms had gone under, and working part-time as a paralegal for the courthouse. Him, Mercer had figured, was the kind of voter he needed to reach. He tipped his mug at Mercer. "One more of those, I'm tipsier than a drunk on a toadstool."

A flash of humor flitted across his face and vanished again. Then he frowned and left to sit alone, looking out the window. Mercer wasn't sure what Roulund thought of life here, but he was pretty sure the only thing the lawyer was going to miss was his mom.

He pushed open the door. Oregon Required He Share the Results

Mercer's clinic would stay open, but Measure 3 would not be the last he would have to worry about. In July the Oregon Legislature passed the Oregon Right To Know Act, requiring all large farms to report on their pesticide use. And in October the statewide farmers' cooperative Pacific Fertilizer announced that it would shutter its decades-old Rockland plant; the last regularly scheduled freight train stopped coming. That November Mercer's town of Oakridge had its first election on whether to pull out of the Pacific Cascade Electric Cooperative, the rural utility, and join the larger Eugene Water & Electric Board.

These matters had everything to do with Mercer's business and all its potential and none at all with whether candidates from either party were worth voting for. He voted for conservative candidates every election cycle, but his consensus was always that extremism was creeping in from both sides. A conservative could compare Obama's health-care policy with the Gestapo's worst, but it was becoming as hard to find a liberal who didn't openly disparage the notion of a sovereign citizenry.

In 1896, a trio of Frenchmen led by Meyer Pollock started the Detroit Lubricant Company to make multi-purpose cooking lard. Except lard turned out to be poor cooking grease, producing inedible and indigestible meals at rock-bottom temperatures and smoking hot ones at stovetop heat. Still, Detroit Lubricant thought it had have something, and over the next thirty years it advertised, sold, and traded recipes to big-name cooks and business folks across the country who couldn't figure out what to do with its product.

Nothing helped. Lard was still lardy.

In the late 1920s, the Pasteurized Milk Dealers Association reached out to Detroit Lubricant. The dealers had cream they needed to do something with, and they'd heard recipes from the company's customers that might help. So for two years the PMDA bought lard and tried a few of the stupidest-sounding ones out: Solomon Epstein tried frying it in eggs with ketchup and Worcestershire; Robert Dedrick stretched it across a rack and secured it like a turkey before covering it with a dry rub of smoke and salt. After hundreds of these failed experiments, William Overholt came up with one that finally worked, even with Detroit Lubricant pale brown lardy lard: instead of oils, fats, and greases, these hamburgers had water.

It was a miserable product of beiges and browns and-beyond everything-elasticky flavorlessness. But the United States was in the Great Depression, and speaking of graying, the decades of ragtime and flappers had given way to the radio and bread lines. Frozen cattle carcasses still hadn't completely replaced barrel bacon, and the idea of a mushy, canned economy hamburger, all for fifteen cents, had a seductive utility. (And the bonus that the vaguely meaty flavor sticks to the roof of your mouth just long enough to make you feel like you might still be chewing something.) Hamburger meat--at least, frozen hamburger meat manufactured by Detroit Lubricant--became an indelible part of American diet, on a par with television, factories, and Coca-Cola.

His chest loosened. For a long moment he just sat and thought about the folks out in the county, most of them patients he would never see, worrying about the ER at the same time their kids were staying up late waiting to see if their proposition had passed. If they'd lost, they would have driven seventy miles for care. They would have had to fly to San Francisco or evolve an entirely new class of local doctors. How much could that have cost?

His cell buzzed. A text:

R U happy now :)?

He puzzled over it for a second. He wasn't sure how to answer, so he didn't. The hospital would keep its doors open. Nobody was going to lose the clinic or their home or the family that lived in it. All those people out in the county—none of them would have to change a thing. He sat back and let the exhaustion of the night wash over him at last, and settled in to go to sleep with a smile on his face.

He woke sometime later to his wife shaking his shoulder. "Drive," she said.

In the parking lot, the sign that usually warned of Flu Shots / Vaccinations Coming Soon was now replaced by a single word, hastily stenciled:

Congratulations.

In his rearview mirror, the letters on the sign looked like they were shifting in the headlights of a dozen cars lined up in the pre–dawn dark. The last thing he'd expected was still happening. He turned the car around and drove the wrong way on the one-way street, letting himself pass each glowing car as the sun came up around it. Somewhere past the last intersection before the highway a crowd had started to gather. He rolled down the window as he passed, though he didn't know what to say, and the crowd lifted its voices and wished him a happy new year. He kept going until he was out of town, until the last of the rural houses flickered past and then went dark behind him. Only then did he allow himself to slow and the adrenaline to fade. Only then did he find his phone and text back:

Thank you.

"They'd have sent all the patients to me," he told his wife, when she asked what was wrong. "The whole damn county. I was ready to break even. Now—"

"Now what?" She put her hands on his shoulders, and he turned and held her tightly. "If the hospital closes, we lose our clinic too, remember?"

He nodded, but she could feel that he was still thinking about the vote, and the stubbornness behind it. She would find out later that he had seen the same pattern in the precinct returns that others had: every precinct that voted against the levy had at least one doctor. Most of the doctors had voted in Ashland, where the voting machines had gone down that morning and the poll workers had gone home, leaving the polls closed. No one had known who would count the ballots of the two hundred Ashland residents who hadn't voted elsewhere. Now it was too late.

The first she knew of it was when Dr. Mercer called her from the clinic before dawn. "You'd better come in," he said. Only two people had called in sick.

When she walked into the exam room he was gathered with the staff in a circle, passing out handwritten schedules. "We're going to open the clinic an hour early," he said. "We're going to take anyone who walks in. We're not turning anyone away, got it?"

Last year just over 100 hospitals in the United States closed. Three of them were in Oregon. Among rural hospitals, closures have become more common since 2010, when healthcare reform created incentives for hospitals to form accountable care organizations. That allowed some larger health systems to expand by buying or affiliating with rural hospitals. The increase in market share brought revenue from more patients and better, higher-paying contracts with commercial health plans. Meanwhile, uncompensated care - the cost of treating patients without insurance or other means to pay - dropped slightly for rural hospitals as more Americans gained access to insurance under the Affordable Care Act. And over the past decade 21 states, including Oregon, have adopted Medicaid expansion - another provision of the ACA. States that did boosted coverage and income for more than 12 million often low-income Americans, including anyone making less than 138% of the federal poverty line. On the news that night they gave the usual updates on ISIS, the Cubs. In Washington, D.C., Congress was planning a lame-duck session to save a hospital.

That didn't bring to mind the regional hospital just across the county line that would close if the appeal didn't reach the Oregon Supreme Court.

Mercer sat in front of the television, turning to his wife and then back to the screen again.

In the next state over, 1,160 miles away, the hospital board in Rochester, Minnesota, considered closing its rural hospitals, the hospitals that stood at the forefront of their state's rural health revolution. In its 1944 annual report, Mayo Clinic would boast of its "scientific organization and an extraordinary esprit de corps." In 2013, Mayo Clinic estimated that it added $10 billion to the U.S. economy.

The city had 81,000 permanent residents. No public or private clinic had been built there since the early 1960s. Everyone considered it a rural town; Rochester looked like what rural Oregon wanted to become. But by 2014, the hospitals were losing money. The board was getting ready to decide which three of the six should close.

The University of Minnesota Hospital in Minneapolis closed in 1986. In 2004, after two decades of bad financial years, the board announced that it would close fifteen hospitals in rural Minnesota. In 2001, a state court in Virginia found Carilion Roanoke Community Hospital not guilty of misusing its public-hospital status.

Before the 1980s, hospitals could only avoid being taxed if they served the poor and the uninsured in need. In Minnesota, the state required a hospital to serve the "poor" and "medically indigent." The district court found that Virginia law didn't specify a precise definition.

Again, Paul Mercer had expected it. But now it was real, and he was sickened, as if someone had physically taken something from him. How could a community let this happen? It was impossible. As far as he could understand, the only way this would be good for anyone is if you owned a hospital and you wanted to squeeze rural hospitals out of business.

He went home and got into bed. His wife told him to get up and have a drink with her. She had vodka. He didn't like vodka. And he was tired. But he was also too afraid to sleep. For three hours he lay in the dark, eyes open, replaying the day he'd first gotten the idea of opening an urgent-care clinic in a rural county.

He'd been working as an ER doctor at a big hospital in Yakima, Washington, in 2008. It was a front-line job, a couple of hours a day of crisis management responding to heart attacks and strokes, which Paul Mercer saw as the fun part, along with gunshot wounds and severed limbs. The hours were easy enough, four nights on, one night off, just before rush hour so he wouldn't be catching the worst of the traffic. But other than that, the work was monotonous—patients in the waiting room of the waiting room; the boredom he had gone into medicine to get away from. There were some days he felt as if he were working in a DMV, just that instead of car registrations the people wanted Percocet.

He read a study that showed that patients, on average, left the waiting room in thirty-six minutes when they came in for open-heart surgery. The average wait time in the ER was five-and-a-half hours, a wait time, he read, that was getting worse every year, partly because of the number of uninsureds, partly because of the complexity of health care.

Paul Mercer had something better, he thought. It would be simple. The doctor would see each patient alone, one by one, face-to-face, and not through a glass wall from which no sounds could be heard. He closed the door behind him and didn't look back."Rural life and the hospital are inextricably connected," says Dr. Paul Swankoski, a critical-care specialist at Aurora Health Care in Wisconsin and chair of Rural Health for the American Academy of Family Physicians. "Go on the Internet and search any rural hospital that's closed and search for the effects on the community. They are all the same. There's a ripple effect, with impacts on businesses and schools, and the property values plummet and jobs are lost. It's not even a question. It's been studied and studied and studied."

There is a well-oiled machine of statistics and studies and newspaper articles—some of it myth, some of it true—that describes hospitals closing one after another as their communities disintegrate around them. "Fifty-one hospitals closed between 2000 and 2009," says Mark Holmes, head of the National Center for Rural Health Works, whose reports have often formed the basis of these tales.

But it's 2010 now, not 2009. And while the hospital in Prineville closed for good last March, the one in Grant County, as I flipped up my old cell phone to answer across the room, was not. By a few hundred dollars it didn't.

From the roof you can see the surrounding mountains ringed with aspens, now turning yellow, and a few ranches near the John Day River. Grant County has over 2,500 square miles of public land. On the other side of the driveway, a white-and-maroon sign proclaims that the hospital is a center of healing and wellness: For all we know, for all we care, we serve our neighbors and their families. Memorial is designated a critical-access hospital, a federal designation for rural medical facilities no more than thirty-five miles from the next facility: what the hospital calls the last mile of health care. Many communities depend on their rural hospitals, but rural hospitals are struggling. There are two problems. The first is practical: at least from a medical standpoint, a lot of what rural hospitals provide can be done somewhere else, for less money, and probably with better service. The second is demographic: the population of each rural county has an average age of 50—a decade older than the last census, and three decades older than the country as a whole. As the population grays, the demand for services goes up, but so does the cost. Even now, fifty-one of the county's seventy-one critical-access hospitals across the state post annual deficits—and that's exaggerating the number by counting a few that are also tri-county regional hospitals. By 1973, when the Oregon legislature began to pass the nation's most generous laws regarding the right to die, the idea that pain was something to be embraced was already breaking apart. A surgeon named Jacque Kervancur wrote in Excuses for Dying that medical technology needed to catch up with people's desires to forgo treatment: "Doctors cannot see themselves as beacons of hope in a great horde of frightful suffering without closing their eyes and ears. This seeing and hearing is exceedingly painful to the average practitioner, who is orientated toward the 'cure.'" The same year, the Oregon Hospice Association received a $1.46 million federal grant to train caregivers to treat patients' pain symptoms without asking the ethical virtue of continuing a given treatment. This is a direct descendant of today's widely accepted "total pain" model, which not only includes physical suffering but also acknowledges "emotional pain, social pain, and existential pain" in any patient's suffering.

Underlying this expansion of pain was a fundamental change in how medical researchers understood its biology: they could see the path of nerve pathways along which pain traveled from the damaged part of the body to the brain, where a patient recognized it as pain. This meant pain was real, tangible, like a fever or an infection. It also opened the possibility of controlling it, of managing the experience as a compassionate physician ought to do. In 1985, Oregon passed a voter bill of rights that created a new medical–legal category of patients who need not be resuscitated. By the end of the 1980s, though, voluntary efforts to get Oregon hospitals to adopt "do not resuscitate" policies had largely failed, and the medical, religious, and insurance lobbies planned to fight state legislation to do the same. To break a legislative logjam over who would make end-of-life decisions, a professor of biology and philosophy named Elizabeth Watson and a bevy of other volunteers gathered signatures to place what would become the Death with Dignity Act on the 1994 ballot. It passed. It was again placed before Oregon voters in 1997, as a result of an expensive effort to repeal the law led by the Oregon Medical Association and the Roman Catholic Church. Sometimes he'd see Mr. Santorelli from the nursing home, Ms. Robinson from up near the Summit, or someone he didn't know. Most of the time everyone but Mr. Santorelli had voted for the measure, but the clerk told him that wasn't always a guarantee.

Millie at the nursing home said you could count on younger people doing what they were told, even about voting. Everybody knew you had to do what they told you. Doc Silvers had said at church that young people were fine kids, but they were gonna have no hospital unless they got their heads on straight.

Mr. Santorelli said he'd been wrong before. Last year Dr. Silvers had said their weakest precinct two months before the election, and when the votes came in, he'd ruled again. But Millie didn't think Dr. Silvers would be wrong twice. This thing was way bigger than the baseball game with the county seat.

The nurse at the jail took in the fresh sandwiches Dave brought—it was his treat when he did the ballots cause nobody except his wife ever brought him anything. They shared while the other inmates shuffled by. Typical Tuesday: Millie got brought in for ten p.m., Mr. Santorelli made his afternoon curfew, and nobody else was due until morning. Late delivery for a Tuesday.

Dave picked up the two blank blue ballots Millie slept with off the nurse's desk along with his green grant-measure one and headed for his pickup. The rest of the voters had voted on Election Day. This was the special day he looked forward to. No one would ever know about this one ballot. No one ever looked for these. He burned Millie's originals in the ashtray when he got home and put his green ballot in his mailbox for the one o'clock pickup.
